extraction.name: PIQA
extraction.description: A benchmark dataset for evaluating and studying physical commonsense understanding in natural language models.
extraction.creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
extraction.publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Annotators were prompted with links to instructables to inspire them to construct a physical goal and a valid solution, along with a subtle permutation to make the solution invalid.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The dataset is inspired by instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The dataset was cleaned of stylistic artifacts and trivial examples using the AFLite algorithm.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were asked for a physical goal, a valid solution, and a trick (an incorrect solution).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Examples with low agreement during validation were removed from the data.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Reporting bias was observed when using unconstrained prompts, as people favored prototypical solutions.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking progress in physical commonsense understanding.

name.evidence: In this paper, we introduce the task of physical commonsense reasoning and a corresponding benchmark dataset Physical Interaction: Question Answering or PIQA .

description.evidence: In this work we introduce the Physical Interaction: Question Answering or PIQA benchmark for evaluating and studying physical commonsense understanding in natural language models.

creator.evidence: Yonatan Bisk1;2;3;4 Rowan Zellers1;4 Ronan Le Bras1 Jianfeng Gao2 Yejin Choi1;4

publisher.evidence: Copyright c2020, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org).

inLanguage.evidence: all data was collected in English.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: Specifically, annotators were asked to glance at the instructions of an instructable and pull out or have it inspire them to construct two component tasks. They would then articulate the goal (often centered on atypical materials) and how to achieve it. In addition, we asked them to provide a permutation to their own solution which makes it invalid, often subtly

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: Specifically, annotators were asked to glance at the instructions of an instructable and pull out or have it inspire them to construct two component tasks.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: Our dataset is inspired by instructables.com, which provides users with instructions on how to build, craft, bake, or manipulate objects using everyday materials.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: The dataset is further cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm introduced in (Sakaguchi et al. 2020; Sap et al. 2019) which is an improvement on adversarial filtering

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: annotators are asked for 1. a physical goal, 2. a valid solution, and 3. a trick. The trick should sound reasonable, but be wrong often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. This often meant that correct examples were removed that required expert level knowledge of a domain

rai:dataBiases.evidence: We initially experimented with asking annotators for (task, tool) pairs via unconstrained prompts, but found that reporting bias swamped the dataset. In particular, when thinking about how to achieve a goal, people most often are drawn to prototypical solutions

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We introduce a new dataset, PIQA , for benchmarking progress in physical commonsense understanding.
